title: La Passion de Falconetti: de Pantin à Buenos Aires
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: L'Enfance, Pantin et la Corse ancestrale

stops.name: Pantin, the birth at the gates of Paris
stops.campa: On 21 July 1892, in the workers' commune of Pantin at the northeastern gate of Paris, Renée Jeanne Falconetti is born to Paul Pierre Falconetti of Sermano in Corsica and Lucie Lacoste of Cahors. The household is poor; the canals and factory smoke of the Seine banlieue stand around the cradle. The face that will one day carry the whole suffering of France onto a white screen opens its eyes first here, among freight yards, an island child born on the mainland, marked from the start for fire.
suggested_refs: Acte de naissance, Pantin, 21 juillet 1892
Hélène Falconetti, 'Falconetti' (Éditions du Cerf, 1987)

stops.name: Sermano, Corsica: the ancestral village
stops.campa: The name comes from Sermano, a granite village of the Bozio above Corte, where her father Paul Pierre was born in 1851 among chestnut groves and the old polyphonic mass, the paghjella that mourns and exults in one breath. The child of Pantin carries the island in her blood: the black-eyed severity, the pride that will make her walk out of the Comédie-Française, the capacity for absolute ordeal. Corsica gave France an emperor; from this hamlet it gives France the face of its saint. The village keeps the name Falconetti, little falcon, the bird that does not look away.
suggested_refs: Sermano village, Bozio, Haute-Corse, photographs
Geneanet record of Paul Pierre Falconetti, b. Sermano 1851

stops.name: Paris, the convent boarding school
stops.campa: From 1905 the girl boards with the nuns, her brother Charles nearby, five years behind convent walls. The sisters teach her catechism and posture and oppose absolutely her ambition for the stage: the theatre being, they say, a house of perdition. The irony is already written: the pupil they discipline on her knees in chapel will kneel again, twenty years on, on the stone floor of Rouen's tribunal, and the Church that forbids her the boards will one day censor her masterpiece. The rite of the convent is the first rehearsal of the Passion.
suggested_refs: Hélène Falconetti, 'Falconetti' (Éditions du Cerf, 1987)

stops.name: Paris, the Conservatoire d'art dramatique
stops.campa: In 1912 she takes the courses of Maurice de Féraudy to prepare the Conservatoire, and the following year passes to Silvain, the old tragedian of the Comédie-Française who has formed generations of players. Against the nuns, against poverty, she chooses the boards. In the rehearsal rooms of the rue du Conservatoire she learns the alexandrine and the mask of comedy: the very make-up and pose that a Danish director will one day strip from her like a shell to find what was always underneath. The apprenticeship is in artifice; the destiny is in its removal.
suggested_refs: Portrait photographs of the young Falconetti, c. 1912-1916

stops.name: Théâtre de l'Odéon, the debut
stops.campa: In 1916, with France at war and the guns of Verdun audible in the nation's sleep, she enters the Odéon and makes her debut in L'Arlésienne: Daudet's play about a woman never seen, a face never shown. She plays for houses of soldiers on leave, men who will return to the trenches carrying her voice. The heroines of Saint-Georges de Bouhélier follow. The republic of the boards receives her in wartime, and the war is her first audience: she learns to hold the gaze of men acquainted with death.
suggested_refs: Programme, Théâtre de l'Odéon, L'Arlésienne 1916

stops.name: Comédie-Française, the sociétariat refused
stops.campa: In 1924 the House of Molière takes her in: she is Rosine in Le Barbier de Séville, Bettine in Musset. Within a year she walks out. The most consecrated stage in France cannot hold the Corsican falcon; hierarchy, seniority, the dust of the repertoire, she refuses them all and returns to the boulevard, to the light comedies and the music-hall glitter. The gesture is prophetic: she abandons the national temple of the word for the place where a silent film will find her. The saint must first refuse the church that is offered.
stops.quote: Quelle triste maison que le Théâtre-Français. J'étais aussi trop indépendante pour me soumettre à la hiérarchie désuète.
stops.quote_source: Falconetti, quoted in the French biographical record (fr.wikipedia.org, after Hélène Falconetti)
suggested_refs: Comédie-Française registres, pensionnaires 1924-1925

stops.name: Théâtre de Paris: La Garçonne
stops.campa: 12 July 1926, rue Blanche: she is Monique Lerbier in La Garçonne, the stage version of Victor Margueritte's scandalous novel of the free woman: the book that cost its author the Légion d'honneur. Falconetti in cropped hair and men's tailoring is the modern woman incarnate, the soubrette of the boulevards at the height of her celebrity: perfume, jewels, a limousine at the stage door, the gambling tables after midnight. The house is full. Somewhere in the dark of such a house, a season hence, a pale Dane will sit down and look at her the way no one has looked.
suggested_refs: La Garçonne, Victor Margueritte, stage adaptation, Théâtre de Paris 1926
Publicity photographs of Falconetti as Monique Lerbier

stops.name: Théâtre de Paris, Dreyer in the audience
stops.campa: Carl Theodor Dreyer, come to France to film the trial of Jeanne d'Arc, has considered Lillian Gish and Madeleine Renaud. Then he goes to a boulevard theatre and watches a comedienne in a light play. He sees nothing the audience sees. He goes backstage, and returns the next day, and afterward he testifies: behind the make-up, behind the pose and the ravishing modern appearance, there was something: a soul behind that façade. It is the annunciation scene of French cinema: the prophet recognizes the martyr in the soubrette, the way the voices found a shepherd girl at Domrémy.
suggested_refs: Carl Th. Dreyer's account of finding Falconetti (interviews, reprinted in Criterion editions)

stops.name: Champs-Élysées, the apartment, the unmade face
stops.campa: The day after the performance Dreyer calls at her apartment near the Champs-Élysées. He asks her to remove her make-up. In the bare afternoon light he studies the naked face of a thirty-four-year-old boulevard star: the wide brow, the heavy-lidded devouring eyes, the skin that will take the close-up like a landscape takes weather. He tells her there will be no make-up in his film, no wigs, no mercy of soft focus. She listens, and consents. In that drawing room the contract of the Passion is sealed: she gives him the face, knowing and not knowing what he will do with it.
suggested_refs: Dreyer's screen tests of Falconetti, 1926-27 (lost)
carlthdreyer.dk collaborator dossier

stops.name: Studios de Billancourt, the shoot begins in Rouen-on-the-Seine
stops.campa: May 1927. At the Billancourt studios on the Seine, Hermann Warm and Jean Hugo have raised an enormous concrete Rouen: castle, tribunal, cemetery, stake, a single octagonal citadel built whole so that the actors live inside the year 1431. Dreyer shoots in sequence, day by day through the trial, as the trial itself unfolded. Seven million francs, and in the end two hundred and seventy-six thousand feet of film, will be consumed. She arrives in a white chauffeured limousine, in furs and jewels; she crosses the studio door and puts on the coarse tunic of the prisoner. Every morning the same descent: from 1927 into the cell.
suggested_refs: Hermann Warm and Jean Hugo set designs and maquettes
Production photographs, Studios de Billancourt 1927

stops.name: Billancourt, the rite of the knees and the takes
stops.campa: Dreyer's direction is an ordeal administered as liturgy. He takes the cushions away and keeps her kneeling on the stone floor until the pain stops being acted. He shoots the same seconds of anguish take after take after take, wearing the performance down past technique, past pride, to the bare nerve. The close-ups are made behind screens, the set closed, the director's voice low and relentless. He is not cruel for cruelty: he is extracting a martyrdom, as an inquisitor extracts a confession, and she, who could leave, stays. Between them, in silence, the film's terrible bargain holds: he asks for everything, and she gives it.
suggested_refs: Frame enlargements: the interrogation close-ups of Falconetti
Accounts of the shoot in Dreyer scholarship (David Bordwell, 'The Films of Carl-Theodor Dreyer')

stops.name: Billancourt, Artaud beside her: the monk Massieu
stops.campa: Among the granite faces of the judges one face is tender: Antonin Artaud, poet of the theatre of cruelty, plays Frère Massieu, the young monk who pities the prisoner. In the film he leans toward her with the only compassion Rouen affords, her one gentle neighbor in a tribunal of tormentors. Two martyrs of performance stand a hand's breadth apart: she who will give everything to one film and never film again, he who will burn his mind for the theatre and end in the asylum at Rodez. The lens holds them together for a few frames: the two most extreme faces France ever lent the screen.
suggested_refs: Still: Artaud as Massieu leaning toward Falconetti's Jeanne
Antonin Artaud, 'Le Théâtre et son double' (1938)

stops.name: Billancourt, the shaving of the head
stops.campa: Near the end, as the trial reaches its degradation, comes the scene written into her contract from the first: the head shaved to the skull before the camera and the assembled crew. The clippers pass; the boulevard star's hair falls on the concrete of the false Rouen. Her tears are real and are filmed. Around her the electricians and carpenters stand uncovered and silent, and some of the men weep; witnesses say the studio was like a place of execution. Nothing is acted. The film records an actual sacrifice, the moment the actress and the saint become indistinguishable: the exact point on which the whole legend of cinema turns.
suggested_refs: The head-shaving sequence, La Passion de Jeanne d'Arc (1928)
Production stills of the shaving scene

stops.name: Copenhagen, Palads Teatret: the world premiere
stops.campa: 21 April 1928: the Passion is shown first not in France but in Dreyer's Copenhagen, at the Palads Teatret. The Danes see what no one has seen: a film of faces alone, the whole judicial murder of France's saint carried on the naked features of a Parisian comedienne. The astonishment is immediate and permanent: critics write that they have seen not a performance but a soul photographed. France's greatest film opens in exile; the pattern is set. Everything about this work, its maker, its premiere, its future graves and resurrection, will belong to the north, as its heart belongs to France.
suggested_refs: Palads Teatret premiere programme, April 1928
Danish press notices, April 1928

stops.name: Paris, the archbishop's scissors
stops.campa: Before France may see its own Passion, the film is put on trial. The Archbishop of Paris demands cuts; the government censors demand more. The judges of 1431 sit again in 1928: churchmen alarmed by clerical faces filmed without flattery, officials uneasy at a Danish Protestant handling the newly canonized saint. Dreyer's print is shortened by order, scene by scene, and he protests in vain. The film has begun its own via crucis: condemned by an ecclesiastical court, mutilated before the crowd, exactly in the pattern of its subject. The canon is precise: what was done to Jeanne is done to the film of Jeanne.
suggested_refs: Offscreen: 'The Passion of Joan of Arc: Censorship and Rediscovery'

stops.name: Paris, Cinéma Marivaux: the French premiere
stops.campa: 25 October 1928, boulevard des Italiens: the cut film finally opens in Paris at the Cinéma Marivaux. Even censored it overwhelms. The city that shaved her head in effigy at Billancourt now watches her burn nightly on the boulevard. The critics reach for the vocabulary of miracle; the word appears that will follow her forever: that this is the greatest performance ever recorded. Falconetti herself is already elsewhere, on the boards, in the casinos. She has one face in the churches of cinema and another at the gaming tables, and she will never allow the two to meet again.
suggested_refs: Cinéma Marivaux premiere notices, RetroNews press archive
Poster, La Passion de Jeanne d'Arc, 1928

stops.name: Berlin, the UFA fire: the negative burned
stops.campa: 6 December 1928. In Berlin, at the UFA works, fire takes the original negative of the Passion: the master image of Falconetti's face, months old, destroyed. The film is burned at the stake as its heroine was, within the year of its birth. Dreyer, believing the true version lost forever, sits down with his editor Marguerite Beaugé and rebuilds the film shot by shot from the outtakes: a second body assembled from relics, the takes his ordeal had multiplied at Billancourt now redeeming the work. Every retake he forced from her becomes a resurrection in waiting.
suggested_refs: Far Out: 'How The Passion of Joan of Arc was accidentally destroyed'

stops.name: Paris, the second burning
stops.campa: Within the year, fire finds the film again: the reconstructed second negative, Dreyer's version built from outtakes, is destroyed in a laboratory blaze in 1929. Twice condemned, twice burned: the film has now outdone its own subject, who was burned once. For half a century the Passion will circulate only in mutilated prints, censored copies, dupes of dupes, its true face as lost as Jeanne's ashes in the Seine. Dreyer will die in 1968 believing his original gone forever. The tomb is sealed; the world settles down to worship a damaged relic, not knowing the body itself lies whole in the north, waiting.
suggested_refs: Criterion Collection essay, The Passion of Joan of Arc

stops.name: Paris, Théâtre de l'Avenue: the fortune staked
stops.campa: She never films again. Dreyer announces a sequel, Catacombes; it is never made; no camera will ever be worthy of the face again, and she knows it. In 1929 she buys the Théâtre de l'Avenue near the Champs-Élysées and pours her fortune into it, her own house, her own repertoire: Juliette ou la Clé des songes, La Dame aux camélias, Phèdre. The house devours her money as Dreyer devoured her takes. The woman who refused the Comédie-Française builds her own temple and is ruined by it, splendidly, in the only style she has: everything staked, nothing withheld.
suggested_refs: Programmes, Théâtre de l'Avenue, 1929-1930s

stops.name: Monte-Carlo, the tables
stops.campa: Monte-Carlo knows her twice: as the triumphant Lorenzo of Lorenzaccio on the stage of its theatre, and as the gambler under the chandeliers next door. The canon is frank about it: the fortunes lost at the tables, the jewels that go the way of the theatre. She plays baccarat as she played Jeanne: absolutely, past prudence, to the last chip. Those who saw her gamble said she seemed to be testing something: as if having once given everything and survived, she must keep proving that loss cannot touch her. The casino takes what Billancourt left. She is stripping herself for the exile to come.
suggested_refs: Lorenzaccio, Théâtre de Monte-Carlo, programme and notices

stops.name: Switzerland, the lake years
stops.campa: Ruined in Paris, she withdraws in the later 1930s to Switzerland, sustained by the financier Henri Goldstuck, her protector and friend. On the lake shore the greatest face of the century lives in furnished quiet: the theatre gone, the fortune gone, the film she will not speak of burning and unburning in cinémathèques far away. Then the protector dies, and the money dies with him, and the war comes down over Europe like a shutter. From the terrace above the water she watches France fall in the summer of 1940. Neutral ground is a ledge, not a home; the falcon must cross the ocean.
suggested_refs: BnF Fonds Falconetti, Swiss correspondence and bank papers

stops.name: Geneva, the leaving of Europe
stops.campa: In 1942, with France occupied whole and the continent closing like a fist, she leaves Europe. The woman who incarnated the saint of French resistance cannot remain in a France that has surrendered; the canon reads her flight as the film's logic continued: Jeanne does not live under occupation. She quits Switzerland with what little the tables and the theatres have left her, crosses the ruins of her fortune, and turns her face to the Atlantic. She is forty-nine years old. She will never see France again: not the boulevards, not Billancourt, not Sermano. The exile of the face begins.
suggested_refs: BnF Fonds Falconetti, papers of the departure

stops.name: Rio de Janeiro, landfall in the New World
stops.campa: The Atlantic crossing ends under the Sugarloaf: Brazil, first ground of the New World, 1942. Rio receives another of Europe's fleeing artists: the harbor is full of them, the shipboard trunks of a drowned continent. She pauses here on the Brazilian ledge of exile, a Frenchwoman without France, the face of Jeanne d'Arc anonymous among the refugees. But the French of South America have their capital further south, where Louis Jouvet's exiled troupe plays and the émigré colony keeps the language alight. She takes ship again, down the coast of the continent, toward the silver river.
suggested_refs: Passenger records, wartime Atlantic crossings to Brazil (BnF Fonds Falconetti)

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Dársena Norte: the arrival
stops.campa: In 1943 she lands at Buenos Aires and settles for good: the city of the Libertadores, the Paris of the south, the last capital of free French speech. Here the exile colony gathers: actors, writers, the France Libre committees, Jouvet's troupe passing through with Molière in its baggage. She comes ashore with almost nothing: a name that means everything in the dark of cinemas and little at the port. The city receives her as it receives all the century's shipwrecked. She does not know it, but she has arrived at her last city, the one where she will die and be buried among strangers.
suggested_refs: Photographs of wartime Buenos Aires port, Dársena Norte

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the recitals of the colony
stops.campa: For the French of Buenos Aires she returns to the stage: she directs and performs Claudel's L'Échange and Cocteau's Les Monstres sacrés: sacred monsters, the play named for what she is. In borrowed halls, before audiences of exiles who weep at the sound of the alexandrine, the woman of the one film gives recitals of the French word. The colony knows who sits among them; the whisper crosses the room: c'est la Falconetti, c'est Jeanne. On these far southern boards the national voice is kept burning through the occupation, a sanctuary lamp tended at the antipodes of Rouen.
suggested_refs: Paul Claudel, L'Échange, Buenos Aires staging
Jean Cocteau, Les Monstres sacrés, Buenos Aires staging

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the elocution lessons, the poverty
stops.campa: The war ends; the exile does not. She stays on in Buenos Aires and lives thinly, giving elocution and acting lessons to the young French-Argentines: the face that Dreyer filmed teaching children where to place their vowels. The recitals grow rarer, the rooms smaller, the money short. Liberated France does not send for her; the film that made her immortal circulates in mutilated copies with her name misprinted as Maria. She is fifty-three, heavy now, far from every stage that mattered, tending the embers of the language in furnished rooms. The canon does not look away: this is the station of obscurity, and she serves it.
suggested_refs: Hélène Falconetti, 'Falconetti' (Éditions du Cerf, 1987), the Buenos Aires chapters

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the last fast
stops.campa: In the southern spring she undertakes the cure that kills her: a slimming regime of terrible severity, imposed on herself as Dreyer once imposed the stone floor. She means to return to the stage with the old silhouette; the discipline runs past the body's limits, and she does not stop it. Those who keep her canon read the fast plainly: it is the last take, the last mortification of the flesh before the camera of God, self-directed, no one left to call an end to the scene. Jeanne refused food in the English prison. The actress, twenty years after, repeats the gesture until it opens the door.
suggested_refs: Hélène Falconetti, 'Falconetti' (Éditions du Cerf, 1987)

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the death of Falconetti
stops.campa: 12 December 1946. In Buenos Aires, in the first heat of the austral summer, Renée Jeanne Falconetti dies, fifty-four years old, worn through by the fast. The face of the Passion goes out in a furnished room ten thousand kilometers from Pantin. The exile colony buries one of its own; France, busy with its liberation, barely notices. She dies in a city that keeps its dead above ground in marble streets, in mausoleums built like small houses along avenues of stone: a city built to hold a relic until it is called for.
suggested_refs: Death record, Buenos Aires, 12 December 1946
The final close-up of La Passion de Jeanne d'Arc (1928)

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the grave in exile
stops.campa: She is laid in an Argentine cemetery, among the marble avenues of the southern dead, and there she waits fourteen years. The city that keeps its dead in houses keeps her too: a French actress in the necropolis of Buenos Aires, the face of Jeanne d'Arc entombed among strangers. The film, meanwhile, is a ruin worshipped in fragments; the actress, a name in an exile's register. Both bodies, the woman's in the south, the film's in the north, lie in their separate tombs through the same decades, and neither France nor cinema knows that both burials are provisional.
suggested_refs: Hélène Falconetti, 'Falconetti' (Éditions du Cerf, 1987)

stops.name: Paris, Cimetière de Montmartre: the ashes come home
stops.campa: In 1960 the body is raised, given to the fire at last: the fire that took Jeanne, the fire that took the negatives, now taking her gently, as a rite of translation, and the ashes cross the Atlantic home. Her daughter Hélène, keeper of the canon, sees them laid in the sixteenth division of the Cimetière de Montmartre, in the hill of artists above the boulevards where Dreyer first found her. The return journey after death is complete: Pantin's child, Corsica's granddaughter, Buenos Aires's exile, rests in Paris. On the stone, one name, which is a whole national scripture: Falconetti.
suggested_refs: Grave of Renée Falconetti, Cimetière de Montmartre, division 16

stops.name: Dikemark, Asker: the closet in the asylum
stops.campa: 1981. At the Dikemark psychiatric hospital outside Oslo, a janitor clearing a closet finds three film canisters in their original 1928 packaging, addressed to Harald Arnesen, the institution's long-dead director. Why Dreyer's Copenhagen distributor sent them there, no one will ever establish. Inside sleeps the impossible: Dreyer's original uncensored cut of the Passion, the version burned at Berlin, burned again in Paris, mourned by its maker to his grave. For fifty-three years the true face of Falconetti has lain whole in a madhouse cupboard in Norway: the film hidden, like its heroine's voices, where only the mad were listening.
suggested_refs: The Dikemark canisters, Norwegian Film Institute collection
Offscreen: 'Censorship and Rediscovery of a Silent Film Classic'

stops.name: Oslo, the Norwegian Film Institute: the resurrection
stops.campa: The canisters sit unexamined at the Norwegian Film Institute for three years. In 1984 they are opened, and the archivists understand what stands on the bench: the original cut, intact, uncensored, unburned. Risen. New negatives are struck from the asylum print; the mutilated copies of half a century are set aside; the world sees at last the film Dreyer made and the face Falconetti gave, every frame she paid for at Billancourt restored to the light. Thirty-eight years after her death in the city of the southern dead, the resurrection is complete. The film was martyred like its subject, and like its subject it did not stay dead.
suggested_refs: Norwegian Film Institute restoration, 1985
Criterion Collection restoration (2012) and the 2015 digital restoration from the Oslo negative
